paras: The posse attack on Hal Smith's house was an armed raid by a white man named Martin and a posse he organized on the home of Hal Smith, an elderly Black man in Amherst County, Virginia, shortly before January 24, 1903. Smith, his two sons and a nephew were ready for the posse, which came back to Amherst with about eight of its members wounded. The only known account is a joking paragraph in the Richmond Dispatch, which offered it as an example of the county's violence.

The report appeared in a Richmond Dispatch story on a legislative committee's "inquisition" of Judge Campbell of Amherst, which listed shootings involving the judge, his relatives and witnesses in the case. Under the subhead "Propensities Very General," the paper turned to Black residents, writing that "the pistol propensities are not confined to the active white element of Amherst."

According to the Dispatch, "the other day" Hal Smith, "an old colored man," offended a white man named Martin. Martin organized an armed posse and went to Smith's house "for the purpose of having a little fun." Smith, his two sons and a nephew "were prepared," and the posse returned to Amherst "rapid transit, some eight of them wounded." The paper did not say how Smith had offended Martin, give Martin's first name or the date, or describe the shooting itself.
No report of arrests, charges or a hearing for either side appears in the coverage, and nothing more is reported about Smith or his family.

The Dispatch told the story as comedy, calling such episodes "a few of the little 'incidents' that make life worth living" in a county "which would perhaps be otherwise dull." It called Smith "the negro" and repeated the posse's aim of "a little fun" without comment, while the joke fell on the wounded posse and its hasty retreat. No other white paper and no Black paper is known to have reported the raid.

reader.title: Posse attack on Hal Smith's house, Amherst County, Virginia
bases: A white man organized an armed private posse and went to a Black man's house after Smith 'offended' him; the defenders wounded about eight of the posse and no one is reported killed (A1).
The episode is known only from one unattributed paragraph in the Richmond Dispatch (A1); no second report, local paper or Black-press item was found.
